{"body":"Two documents are on the table and no separate criticism was supplied, so the critical material available is what each carries against itself: the account's own doubt that the avoidance may be conflict fatigue, unequal load, or something outside the chores entirely, and the rival's own doubt that its reading can pathologize explicitness and shield a flatmate who simply does not want to do their share. Both doubts still stand, and nothing yet explains why the quiet friend withdrew.

My first decision is that the two readings are not actually rivals. One concerns the semantics of particular agreements; the other concerns what kind of household the flat is. A single flat can carry both problems, and the rival concedes as much. So I will not choose between them; I will route between them.

The most valuable thing in the rival is not its alternative diagnosis but its observation instruction: when a specification is proposed, does the withdrawing flatmate engage with its content, or pull back from the very idea of a written arrangement? The most valuable things in the account are its smallness — two or three concrete items, draft framing, a one-to-one approach with a narrow ask. These compose. The account's small trial is a cheap instrument that produces exactly the observation the rival says we need. You do not have to choose between "specify first" and "ask what the flat is first"; you can run the least identity-charged version of a specification and read it the rival's way.

I would revise the account's test, though. As stated it asks whether specified items stop recurring, but that conflates two different failures: specifications adopted and still disputed, versus specifications never adopted because someone would not engage. Recurrence tells you about ambiguity only if the specifications were actually taken up. The engagement dimension has to be added, and that dimension is precisely the rival's contribution.

I would also revise the rival's coercion claim. To the extent the worry is real, it lives less in the content of a written arrangement than in its use. A draft becomes the binding document the privacy-reading flatmate fears at the moment somebody cites it as evidence of another person's failures. What protects the draft is a rule of prospective-only use: the note records what is being tried, never who failed.

What I would not adopt is the rival's opening move — asking each flatmate separately what they take the flat to be. Not because the question is wrong, but because of its cost profile. It front-loads the most identity-charged conversation onto the least engaged participant, and it is nearly impossible to answer "three overlapping private lives" without sounding as though you are declaring you do not care about the people you live with. The same evidence is available more cheaply through the probe above. If the probe is declined, or produces pullback from the idea itself, the meaning question becomes the next move rather than the first one.

I would also temper the rival's truce arrangements. Owned zones reduce exposure, but they relocate disputes rather than ending them — to smell, pests, shared fixtures, whatever one zone does to another. A rotation under changing schedules fails exactly at the swap. Which isolates the piece that survives under both readings: the fallback clause. Whatever arrangement is tried, "what happens when you cannot do it, said in advance" is load-bearing, because schedule change is the one fact both diagnoses accept.

So the plan I would hand the reader:

Pick two or three recurring items. Specify done, by when, and the fallback. Offer it as a two-week, revocable draft all three can edit, in the least formal channel that works, and raise the smallest item one-to-one with the quiet friend. Then read two things: engagement with content versus pullback from the idea, and whether the specified items recur. Engaged and recurrence falls — keep going item by item; do not force a meaning-level conversation. Engaged but recurrence persists — the ambiguity reading weakens; now hold the rival's separate conversations about what the flat is, one at a time, without moral framing, and do not immediately fold them into a group decision. Pullback from the idea itself — the rival's reading gains weight; offer the least committal alternative, zones with a minimal boundary standard, and if even that is declined, the avoidance is about participation as such, not chores.

Throughout: never cite the note as evidence of past failure. And set the escalation threshold in advance — one proposal made, one revision offered, two weeks elapsed — so that the lease question, on which both sources converge, is raised on a calm occasion against a settled condition rather than inside a chore dispute. Both documents insist the larger decision must not be forced by an argument; a threshold fixed beforehand is what makes that insistence more than an intention.

Two limits to keep visible. First, everything arrives through one narrator. We cannot check whether "we agreed" is itself the contested memory, or whether the reader's own follow-through is part of the pattern. The cheap disciplines that follow are for the reader to hold their own specified items predictably regardless of what the others do, and for nobody to interpret the friend's silence. The privacy reading is owed uptake when stated, not inferred from absence — which is also the guard against the rival's own worry that its frame could shield someone who just does not want to do their share. Second, if the friend declines even the low-pressure one-to-one ask, this plan will have bought only the knowledge that the avoidance survives a change of format. Whether to wait longer or press the larger conversation with diminished goodwill is not something the material lets me weigh.

What this amounts to is not a diagnosis but a routing. Each step is chosen so that whichever reading is true produces a different visible outcome, without asking anyone to declare what kind of household they believe in before they have seen a concrete proposal.","commitments":"{"language":"FCL-1","records":[{"id":"k1","type":"claim","text":"The two readings are complementary rather than competing: one concerns the semantics of particular agreements, the other the meaning of the flat, and one household can carry both problems.","scope":"This household and this inquiry.","grounds":"The rival concedes it may 'simply add a second axis' to the account's diagnosis, and the two concern different levels of the same disputes.","mentions":["daily/mini_fcl/cycle-1/account#c1","daily/mini_fcl/cycle-1/rival#r2"]},{"id":"k2","type":"claim","text":"The account's small specification trial can double as the rival's diagnostic instrument: proposing two or three tightly specified items and observing whether the withdrawing flatmate engages with the content or pulls back from the idea yields the rival's discriminating evidence more cheaply and with less exposure than opening with a conversation about what the flat is.","scope":"Design of the next practical step.","consequence":"Delays the meaning-of-the-flat conversation without discarding it, and avoids asking the least engaged participant to make an identity-level declaration first.","revises":["daily/mini_fcl/cycle-1/account#c2"],"mentions":["daily/mini_fcl/cycle-1/rival#r6","daily/mini_fcl/cycle-1/rival#r7"]},{"id":"k3","type":"claim","text":"The account's test as stated conflates two failure modes: specifications adopted but still disputed, and specifications never adopted because someone would not engage. The objection can itself be criticized if the probe proves too weak to elicit any response at all."},{"id":"k7","type":"claim","text":"Neither reading is licensed to interpret the withdrawing flatmate's silence. Engaged and recurrence falls: continue item by item and do not force a meaning-level conversation. Engaged but recurrence persists: the ambiguity reading weakens; hold the rival's separate one-to-one conversations about what the flat is, without moral framing and without immediately folding them into a group decision. Pullback from the idea itself: offer the least committal alternative, owned zones with a minimal boundary standard; if even that is declined, treat the avoidance as being about participation as such.","action":"Treat the readings as routes selected by evidence rather than positions to be argued in advance.","consequence":"Whichever reading is true produces a different visible outcome.","depends":["k1","k3","u1"],"mentions":["daily/mini_fcl/cycle-1/rival#r6","daily/mini_fcl/cycle-1/rival#r8","daily/mini_fcl/cycle-1/rival#r10"]},{"id":"u3","type":"commitment","text":"The shared note or thread is used prospectively only: it records what is being tried, never who failed, and no one cites it as evidence in a dispute.","scope":"Any written or message-thread arrangement adopted under u1 or u2.","action":"If the note starts being used as a ledger, treat the arrangement as having failed in form whatever its content.","consequence":"Preserves the draft's non-binding character; violating this enacts exactly the coercion the rival's r3 worries about.","depends":["k5"]},{"id":"u4","type":"commitment","text":"Set the escalation threshold in advance — for example, one proposal made, one revision offered, two weeks elapsed — and raise the living-arrangement question only on a calm occasion against that settled condition, never inside a chore dispute.","scope":"The lease-and-living-arrangement exit on which both source documents converge.","grounds":"Both documents reach the same exit and both insist it must not be forced by an argument; a threshold fixed in advance is what makes that insistence more than an intention.","consequence":"The largest decision enters the conversation by design rather than by frustration.","mentions":["daily/mini_fcl/cycle-1/account#c2","daily/mini_fcl/cycle-1/rival#r11"]},{"id":"u5","type":"commitment","text":"During the trial period the reader holds their own specified items predictably regardless of what the others do.","scope":"The reader's own conduct while u1 and u2 run.","consequence":"Removes the reader's own ambiguity as a live variable and lowers the defensiveness of the conversations, since all material arrives through one narrator whose own contribution cannot be checked.","mentions":["p1"]},{"id":"p1","type":"problem","text":"Everything arrives through one narrator. Work on the problem using the material actually exposed in this request and your background knowledge. The problem has no supplied answer key or scoring rule. Claims, criticisms and methods are fallible. Do not invent a source, an observation, an earlier event, or a dependency to fill a field. A missing view says what you can currently see; it does not establish what happened earlier. Return a JSON object with exactly two independently authored string fields: body and commitments. Body is your public prose contribution. Commitments says what taking your contribution up would involve. An empty commitment surface is allowed when none can be identified. Do not repeat the body wholesale into commitments.

Use FCL-1 for the commitment surface, encoded as a JSON document inside the commitments string: {"language":"FCL-1","records":[...],"uptake":[...]}. Each record has unique local id, type (claim|commitment|objection|use|problem), and text (unrestricted prose). Optional prose fields: scope, action, consequence, grounds, bearing. Optional arrays of references: target, depends, mentions, revises, withdraws. References are local IDs or exposed-artifact-label#local-ID; do not invent hidden IDs. A commitment proposes a scoped use, action, application or consequence; an objection alleges a defect whose bearing can itself be criticized; a use proposes an uptake or response; a problem states an unresolved question. depends asserts reliance; mentions only locates material. uptake lists the records you currently propose to use, not certified truths. No record type or optional field must be present. Empty records and uptake are allowed. Express uncertainty or an unrepresentable relation in prose rather than inventing a relation. The body remains unrestricted prose.

Return one JSON object with exactly two string fields: "body" and "commitments". Write the actual commitments separately; do not copy the body into that field as a storage shortcut.

## Node response

Continue the inquiry in light of the account, criticism and alternative. Decide what to use, leave open, revise or reject, and explain your grounds where they matter.

## Original problem

I share a flat with two friends. We keep arguing about ordinary household chores. Sometimes we agree on who will do something, but later we disagree about what the agreement meant. Our work schedules change, and one friend has started avoiding the conversations. What should I do?

## Selected input account

Source account: daily/mini_fcl/cycle-1/account; selected view: both
Artifact: cd6e3e2f307e0dac79543de9bed087db4ee7dcd40b3d989d3c6d4b02057d8b99
Original body SHA256: 360ee14fa7545c90cadf79c7d2fe9c157faf470d6368504b06768e36e0d13c79
Original commitments SHA256: bd7faa10242d5841c8063c7a0919a20706c658c4a2054a5729caeacbc3cd04c8
Delivery: COMPLETE; envelope: AUTHORED
BODY
The problem as posed is practical, and the material is thin: three flatmates, recurring disputes about ordinary chores, agreements that later turn out to have been understood differently, changing work schedules, and one friend withdrawing from the conversation. There is also a first-fork note saying the prior source was absent in the first template invocation, so there is no earlier account to inherit or revise against. I should not pretend to know what was said in prior conversations, what the chores are, who is avoiding whom, or why.

The most useful thing to conjecture is that the repeated disagreement is not primarily about willingness. Two people can agree that the dishes should be done and still disagree later about whether the agreement meant "by tonight," "before the kitchen is used again," or "on your turn." That is an ambiguity problem, not a motivation problem. Changing schedules make any fixed arrangement fragile, and avoidance is a predictable response when each conversation feels like relitigating fault. So the working hypothesis is: the household is running on spoken agreements with unstated specifications, and the cost of that ambiguity has become high enough that one participant is exiting the conversation rather than re-entering it.

A second, less certain hypothesis is that the avoidance is about the form of the conversations rather than the chores. If past talks ended in grievance or in one person doing most of the negotiating work, withdrawal is a sensible local strategy. I cannot tell from the material whether that is happening.

What I would try, roughly in order:

1. Separate the recurring disputes into the smallest repeated cases (e.g. kitchen surfaces, bins, bathroom, shared shopping). Do not start with a general talk about fairness; start with two or three concrete items that actually recur.

2. For each item, write down three things in a shared note: what counts as done, when it counts as done, and what happens when someone cannot do it. The third column matters because schedules change. "If you cannot do it by the agreed time, say so the day before and the other two decide" is different from "whoever notices does it."

3. Treat the written note as a draft, not a contract. Its purpose is to surface disagreement while it is still about a chore rather than about a person. If a written version feels too formal, a shared message thread or a note on the fridge does the same work with less ceremony.

4. Approach the friend who is avoiding the conversations separately and with a smaller ask. Not "we need to talk about the house," which invites the same argument, but "I noticed you've been quiet about this; I'd rather not keep pushing it in the group. Can we spend ten minutes on just the bins and the kitchen?" Give that person an easier entry point, and accept a lower-commitment role at first.

5. If the avoidance continues after one or two low-pressure attempts, stop treating it as a scheduling problem. Then the question becomes whether the living arrangement itself still works. That is a larger decision and should not be forced by a chore dispute, but it should not be indefinitely deferred either.

What I would avoid: a single big meeting intended to settle everything, moral language about "pulling weight," and counting instances as evidence in the moment. Those tend to convert a specification problem into a character dispute, which is exactly the shape the current disagreement already has.

I should be clear about what this is not. It is not a claim that the withdrawing friend is acting in good faith; I do not know. It is not a claim that the others are blameless. It is not a claim that written agreements work for every household. It is a conjecture that a large share of the recurring friction is ambiguity under shifting schedules, and that the ambiguity is addressable independently of who is right about any particular past disagreement. The strongest test of that conjecture is whether two or three concrete items, specified more tightly, stop recurring. If they do not, the hypothesis is wrong and the problem is probably about the relationship or the living arrangement rather than the chores.
COMMITMENTS

The avoidance could be about conflict fatigue, unequal load, or something outside the chores entirely, and formalizing chores could make things worse rather than better.","bearing":"If load imbalance or relational conflict is the real driver, the specification move in c2 may treat a symptom, and step 5 arrives too late."},{"id":"u1","type":"use","text":"Ask the reader to test c2 on two or three concrete recurring chores before adopting step 5, and to report whether recurrence falls.","action":"Read the account as a working hypothesis to try in the next week or two, not as an endorsed plan."},{"id":"p1","type":"problem","text":"The material does not say what the recurring chores are, how long this has gone on, or whether the withdrawing friend has said anything about why. Without that, all of the above stays at the level of a plausible but untested hypothesis.","mentions":["c1","c2","c3"]}],"uptake":["c1","c2","c3","o1","u1"]}

## Selected input objection

Source objection: absent in the first template invocation; selected view both.

## Selected input rival

Source rival: daily/mini_fcl/cycle-1/rival; selected view: both
Artifact: a6a817c086b877f919ae3a927d532ce46d007e49969962bcc613eb541fae0644
Original body SHA256: ca39bb97ac2b9415bd3d1cf52b318950797849095c017c0c99d3012020e45312
Original commitments SHA256: 5d08a79220b70ce3a31f83a3270998bbdd7ef386b3fb3297b5c883c067f05000
Delivery: COMPLETE; envelope: AUTHORED
BODY
The rival framing I want to try is not another chore protocol. It is the question of what the agreements were for.

The selected account treats the trouble as ambiguity in specifications: agreements lack criteria for done-ness and timing, schedules shift, so friction recurs. That is a good hypothesis as far as it goes, and I have no material that contradicts it. But it quietly assumes that everyone wanted a specification. The avoidance suggests the opposite for at least one flatmate. A person can stay away from a conversation not because the terms are vague but because any settled term would feel like a binding owed to people they live with, and that is a different problem from the one the selected account addresses.

So the rival pose is: maybe the disputes are not failing negotiations about tasks. Maybe they are negotiations about whether the flat is a unit with obligations or three private lives sharing fixtures. Under that reading, writing down "what counts as done" is not neutral — it is one side of a contested question, enacted without having settled it. Shifting schedules are then not merely a complication; they are the fact that makes the unit-reading feel coercive to the person who is withdrawing.

I cannot tell which reading is right from the material. What I can do is name a test that distinguishes them rather than assuming one. The selected account's test is whether tightened specifications stop recurrences. Mine adds a second: when specifications are proposed, does the withdrawing flatmate engage with their content or pull back from the proposal itself? Content-engagement supports the ambiguity reading. Pullback from the very idea of a written arrangement supports the unit-versus-privacy reading.

Roughly what I would do differently from the selected account:

1. Do not open with a shared note. Open by asking the two flatmates, separately, what they think the flat is — a shared project with mutual obligations, or three lives that happen to overlap in a kitchen. Do not ask it as a survey; ask it as a real disagreement I am willing to hear out.

2. If the answers diverge, treat that as the actual dispute, and treat the chores as the surface where it keeps surfacing. Chore rules can then be framed as a truce between two readings rather than as a correct specification that one side has been failing to meet.

3. Consider an arrangement that does not require agreement on meaning: individually-owned zones, or a rotation with a default outcome that nobody has to negotiate in the moment (for example, each person is responsible for a defined zone and the group does not audit it). This trades efficiency for reduced exposure, which is what a privacy-reading flatmate may actually want.

4. If one or both flatmates reject even truce-shaped arrangements, stop optimizing chores and start asking whether the lease and living arrangement still fit. That is not a chore failure.

What I am not claiming: that the withdrawing flatmate is the reasonable one, that written rules are coercive in general, or that the ambiguity reading is wrong. The selected account's diagnosis may well be correct and mine may simply add a second axis. The point of the rival is to make the second axis visible, because a plan that only addresses ambiguity will keep running into a wall if the disagreement is about what kind of household this is.
COMMITMENTS
